title: Pre-flop Opens and C-bets from UTG (9-max)
intro: You are UTG in a live 9-max $1/$2 cash game with deep stacks. This lesson walks through opening hand selection, sizing, a dry-board c-bet, and a two-street barrel plan when the turn changes the equity picture.

questions.prompt: Effective stacks 100bb in a 9-max $1/$2 cash game. Folded to you UTG. Which hand is the clearest profitable open?

answers.explanation: KTo is dominated by most of the calling and 3-betting ranges that act behind you in early position. It's a leak from UTG in 9-max.
AJs has strong equity against the calling range, flops well, and unblocks the hands you want villains to continue with. A clear open from UTG.
44 set-mines poorly from UTG because eight players act behind. It plays better in late position where you realize equity more easily.
Q9s is too dominated and too disconnected to open profitably from UTG; it's a late-position hand.

questions.prompt: Standard UTG open sizing in a 9-max live $1/$2 game with deep stacks. What is the most theoretically sound raise size?

answers.explanation: 2x is too small for a live game with many players behind and a high rake. It invites calls and reduces fold equity.
3x ($6 over a $2 BB) is the standard live-cash UTG open. Big enough to thin the field and price out speculative hands, small enough to keep risk manageable.
5x is over-sized and bleeds chips when called by stronger hands. Reserve larger sizes for spots with limpers or specific exploitative reads.
Limping UTG caps your range and gives up the initiative. It's almost always a leak in 9-max cash with no prior action.

questions.prompt: You open AKs from UTG to $6 and only the BB (a passive loose fish) calls. Flop comes Kc 7d 2s. BB checks. What is the most theoretically sound action?

answers.explanation: Checking back forfeits value with top pair top kicker on a dry board. You lose protection and don't get paid by worse Kx and pocket pairs.
A small c-bet (~$4 into $13) maximizes EV: gets thin value from worse Kx and pocket pairs, denies equity to villain's gutshots and overcards, and keeps villain's bluff-catching range wide.
A large c-bet on a dry board folds out the exact hands you want to call (Qx, Jx, small pairs) and only gets called by hands that beat you or have equity against you.
Overbetting AK on K72 rainbow is a clear leak. The board is too dry to need protection sizing, and villain folds out almost every worse hand.

table_state.notes: Villain has been calling wide preflop and folding turn often when missed.

questions.prompt: Same hand: UTG opens AKs to $6, BB (PLF) calls. Flop Kc 7d 2s: you c-bet $4, BB calls. Turn is Th, putting a backdoor flush draw and gutshot straight draws on the board. BB checks. Considering the whole line - flop c-bet AND the turn - what is the most theoretically sound plan?

answers.explanation: Checking back the turn abandons the equity you built with the flop c-bet and lets villain's floats and gutshots realize their equity for free.

answers.text: Small barrel ~1/3 pot for thin value and denial
answers.explanation: A small second barrel (~$7 into $21) keeps folding out the pure air, charges the gutshots and backdoor flush draws, and gets value from Kx and 7x that called flop. Consistent with the small-c-bet, multi-street pressure plan against a PLF's wide calling range.
Overbetting turn on a card that added draws bloats the pot on the exact street where villain's range gets sticky. Reserve overbets for range-nutted spots, not here.
Delaying aggression here is a leak: villain calls flop with too many hands you beat, and you lose value + protection by checking a turn that helps their draws.

table_state.notes: Question spans flop AND turn decisions - the plan is evaluated across both streets.
